safe.title: Safe to delete
safe.blurb: Caches and build output every app rebuilds on its own. No cost.

regen.title: Regenerable
regen.blurb: Comes back on the next build or install. Costs one slow build.

decide.title: Your call
decide.blurb: Real data or tooling. Delete only what you no longer use.

keep.title: Keep
keep.blurb: Needed for current work. Shown so the numbers add up.

locked.title: Managed by macOS
locked.blurb: macOS manages these itself — purged automatically or SIP-protected. Shown for accounting.

entries.label: Claude Desktop local VM image
entries.note: Re-created whenever a Cowork task is linked to this Mac. Grows with use, never shrinks. Quit Claude first.

explain.what: The Linux virtual machine Claude Desktop runs Cowork tasks in: a disk image that grows as tasks install things and never shrinks.
explain.why: It holds nothing of yours — the files a task edits stay in your folders — but Claude has to download and build it again, gigabytes, the next time a Cowork task is linked to this Mac.
explain.after: Claude Desktop recreates the image on the next Cowork task. Quit Claude first so nothing is writing to it.
explain.keep: You use Cowork most days.

entries.label: Claude local-agent session data
entries.note: State and scratch files from Claude Desktop's local-agent (Cowork) sessions. Recreated per session.

explain.what: Working state and scratch files from Claude Desktop's local-agent (Cowork) sessions that already ran.
explain.why: Scratch for finished sessions; nothing reads it back, and each new session starts its own.
explain.after: Gone; the next session starts with an empty folder.

entries.label: Claude Code VM data
entries.note: Files from the sandbox Claude Code in Claude Desktop runs in. Recreated on the next session.

explain.what: Files the sandbox Claude Code in Claude Desktop runs in keeps between sessions.
explain.why: Recreated when the next session starts; your repositories are not in here.
explain.after: The next Claude Code session in Claude Desktop sets the sandbox up again.

entries.label: Staged macOS update download
entries.note: A queued OS update. Re-downloads unless automatic update downloads are turned off in Software Update.

explain.what: A macOS update Software Update has downloaded and staged but not yet installed, usually several GB.
explain.why: Nothing but the pending update lives here, and macOS downloads it again if it still means to install it.
explain.after: Software Update re-downloads it on its schedule; turn off 'Download new updates when available' in System Settings › General › Software Update to stop that.
explain.keep: You are about to install that update anyway.

entries.label: Spotlight index
entries.note: Rebuilds itself if deleted. Keep it small by adding ~/Projects and ~/Library to Spotlight Privacy.

explain.what: Spotlight's search index of the data volume.
explain.why: Deleting it only makes Spotlight rebuild the same index over hours while the Mac runs warm; search is broken meanwhile.
explain.keep: Always. Shrink it by adding folders you don't need indexed to System Settings › Spotlight › Search Privacy.

entries.label: Swap files
entries.note: Virtual memory. Frees itself on restart; nothing to delete.

explain.what: Memory macOS has paged out to disk (the swapfiles) and the sleep image.
explain.why: In use by the running system: it can't be removed and shrinks by itself after a restart.
explain.keep: Always; restart the Mac to reclaim it.

entries.label: ~/Library/Caches
entries.note: Every app's cache, one folder per app — Details lists them. Quit the app first; its next launch will be slower.

explain.what: Every app's cache folder, one per bundle id: thumbnails, downloaded assets, compiled shaders, web caches.
explain.why: By Apple's own definition anything in Caches may be thrown away at any time, and a well-behaved app recreates what it needs.
explain.after: Apps rebuild their caches as you use them; the first launch after is slower, and browsers and Xcode refill theirs quickly.
explain.keep: An app is running and mid-download — quit it first.

entries.label: ~/.cache
entries.note: uv, pip, Hugging Face, Puppeteer, firebase and other CLI tools, one folder each — Details lists them.

explain.what: The XDG cache for command-line tools: uv and pip wheels, Hugging Face model downloads, Puppeteer's browsers, firebase, pre-commit environments and more.
explain.why: By convention ~/.cache is disposable; every tool downloads again what it needs.
explain.after: The next run of each tool downloads again — a model or a browser can be gigabytes, so expect one slow run.
explain.keep: You work offline or on a metered connection and rely on models cached here.

entries.label: App caches (Electron)
entries.note: Slack, Claude, VS Code, Notion, Figma, Discord, Postman… keep web caches next to their data. Rebuilt on the next launch; quit the app first.

explain.what: The web caches Electron apps keep next to their data in Application Support: Cache, Code Cache, GPUCache and the Dawn shader caches.
explain.why: They are browser caches — pages, scripts and shaders the app fetched or compiled. The app's own data (messages, notes, settings) sits beside them and is not touched.
explain.after: Each app refills its cache as you use it; the first launch is slower. Quit the app first, or it may keep writing.
explain.keep: An app is running.

entries.label: ~/Library/Logs
entries.note: One folder per app — Details lists them. Crash reports (DiagnosticReports) and Backspacer's own log are left alone.

explain.what: Log files apps write, one folder each. Backspacer's own log and the DiagnosticReports crash reports are excluded from the sweep.
explain.why: Logs only matter while you're debugging that app, and they regrow with every launch.
explain.after: Apps start fresh logs. If you're reporting a bug to a developer, save that app's log first.
explain.keep: You are about to send a bug report.

entries.label: Trash
entries.note: Emptying here is the same as Finder's Empty Trash.

explain.what: What you moved to the Trash and haven't emptied.
explain.why: You already discarded it; Backspacer only empties the bin.
explain.after: Gone for good, exactly as Finder's Empty Trash. If Finder reports an item in use, empty from Finder.

entries.label: Aerial wallpaper cache
entries.note: Returns if you use an aerial wallpaper. Switch to a static one to keep it gone.

explain.what: The aerial (video) wallpapers macOS downloaded for the desktop and screen saver, hundreds of MB each.
explain.why: macOS downloads a wallpaper again whenever it is selected; the folder is pure cache.
explain.after: Nothing changes unless an aerial wallpaper is active — then it downloads again. Switch to a still wallpaper to keep the space.

entries.label: Homebrew downloads
entries.note: Bottles kept after install. brew cleanup removes the same.

explain.what: Bottles and source tarballs Homebrew downloaded to install formulae and casks, kept after installing.
explain.why: Homebrew only reads them to reinstall the same version; brew cleanup removes them too.
explain.after: A reinstall of the same version downloads again; nothing installed changes.

entries.label: Homebrew orphaned dependencies
entries.infoCmd:
C="$(dirname "$(dirname "$(command -v brew)")")/Cellar"; O=$(brew autoremove -n 2>/dev/null); N=$(printf "%s
" "$O" | grep -v "^==>" | grep .); if [ -z "$N" ]; then echo "No orphaned dependencies."; else printf "%s

" "$O"; printf "%s
" "$N" | while read -r f; do du -sk "$C/${f##*/}" 2>/dev/null; done | awk '{s+=$1} END {printf "Total: %.0f MB", s/1024}'; fi
entries.note: Formulae nothing depends on anymore. Details lists what would go and how much it takes (checked only when you ask — brew is slow).

explain.what: Formulae installed only as dependencies of something you later removed; nothing depends on them now (what brew autoremove finds).
explain.why: Homebrew records why each formula was installed, and these were never asked for by you.
explain.after: Homebrew installs any of them again the moment a formula needs it.
explain.keep: You use one directly — brew install it explicitly and it stops being an orphan.

entries.label: VS Code caches
entries.note: Compiled-code cache, kept extension downloads and logs. Rebuilt on the next launch.

explain.what: VS Code's compiled-code cache, the extension packages (VSIXs) it kept after installing them, and its logs.
explain.why: All three are rebuilt or re-fetched by VS Code itself; extensions and settings live elsewhere.
explain.after: VS Code recompiles its cache on the next launch, a couple of seconds slower once.

entries.label: VS Code dictation models
entries.note: Speech models downloaded the first time you dictate to Copilot. Re-downloaded on demand.

explain.what: Speech-recognition models VS Code downloaded the first time you dictated to Copilot.
explain.why: Downloaded on demand and used by nothing else.
explain.after: The next dictation downloads the model again (a few hundred MB).

entries.label: VS Code workspace storage
entries.note: Per-folder UI state and extension scratch data. You lose 'reopen my tabs' and any extension chat history stored per workspace — never source or settings. Details lists them by project.

explain.what: Per-folder UI state and extension scratch data, one folder per workspace you opened (Details lists them by project).
explain.why: It holds nothing you wrote: open tabs, scroll positions, and whatever extensions cache per workspace — including some chat histories.
explain.after: Each workspace reopens with default tabs and layout; extensions rebuild their scratch data.
explain.keep: An extension's per-workspace chat history matters to you.

entries.label: Xcode DerivedData
entries.note: Build intermediates. Rebuilt on the next build.

explain.what: Build intermediates, indexes and module caches for every project Xcode has opened, one folder each (Details lists them).
explain.why: Purely derived from your source; Xcode's own Clean Build Folder deletes the same thing.
explain.after: The next build of each project is a full one — minutes on a large project — and indexing starts over.
explain.keep: You are mid-debugging on a big project and a full rebuild would cost you.

entries.label: Simulator dyld caches
entries.note: Regenerated on the next simulator boot.

explain.what: The dyld shared caches CoreSimulator builds per runtime so simulators boot faster.
explain.why: Regenerated on the next simulator boot; the runtimes themselves are elsewhere.
explain.after: The first boot of each simulator runtime is slow while its cache is rebuilt.

entries.label: Simulator device contents
entries.itemsCmd: xcrun simctl list devices -j | python3 -c 'import json,sys; d=json.load(sys.stdin)["devices"]; [print(x["udid"], x["name"]+" · "+rt.split(".")[-1].replace("-", " ", 1).replace("-", "."), int(x.get("dataPathSize",0)//1024), sep="\t") for rt,devs in d.items() for x in devs if x.get("isAvailable")]'
entries.deleteItemCmd: xcrun simctl shutdown {key} 2>/dev/null; xcrun simctl erase {key}
entries.deleteCmd: xcrun simctl shutdown all; xcrun simctl erase all
entries.note: Erases installed apps and data but keeps the devices; apps reinstall on the next run. Details lists each simulator so you can erase just one.

explain.what: Each simulator's disk: installed apps, their data and settings, one folder per device (Details lists them).
explain.why: Apps reinstall on the next run, but data you set up inside a simulator — test accounts, photos, sample content — is gone.
explain.after: The devices stay and come back factory-fresh, like Device › Erase All Content and Settings.
explain.keep: A simulator holds test data that took effort to set up.

entries.label: Simulators whose runtime is gone
entries.note: Devices left behind after a runtime was removed. Always safe.

explain.what: Simulator devices whose runtime was deleted; Xcode lists them as unavailable and can't boot them.
explain.why: Nothing can use a device without its runtime, and xcrun simctl delete unavailable is Apple's own command for this.
explain.after: Gone. Xcode creates a new device if you install that runtime again.

entries.label: Simulator runtimes
entries.itemsCmd: xcrun simctl runtime list -j | python3 -c 'import json,sys; d=json.load(sys.stdin); [print(k, v.get("runtimeIdentifier","").split(".")[-1].replace("-", " ", 1).replace("-", ".")+" ("+v.get("build","")+")", int(v.get("sizeBytes",0)//1024), sep="\t") for k,v in d.items() if v.get("deletable")]'
entries.note: One image per iOS version, ~8 GB each. Keep the version you target; Details lists them so you can delete the others one at a time.

explain.what: Simulator runtime images, one per iOS, watchOS, tvOS or visionOS version, several GB each (Details lists them).
explain.why: You need the versions you test against; every other version is a download away.
explain.after: Xcode downloads a runtime again when you choose it in Settings › Components.
explain.keep: The version your app targets and the one on your test device.

entries.label: SwiftUI preview data
entries.note: Simulator state for canvas previews. Rebuilt the next time a preview runs.

explain.what: Simulator state SwiftUI's canvas keeps for previews.
explain.why: Rebuilt the next time a preview runs; contains nothing you wrote.
explain.after: The first preview after is slower.

entries.label: iOS DeviceSupport symbols
entries.note: One folder per iOS version of every device ever plugged in. Details lists them — keep the version on your current phone, delete the rest.

explain.what: Debug symbols Xcode copied from every device ever plugged in, one folder per iOS version and build.
explain.why: Xcode needs the folder matching your device's current iOS to debug on it; the rest belong to versions those devices no longer run.
explain.after: Xcode copies the symbols again (a few minutes) the next time a device on that version connects.
explain.keep: The folder for the iOS version on your current phone.

entries.label: Xcode archives
entries.note: Past App Store / ad-hoc builds with their dSYMs. Needed to symbolicate crash reports for those builds.

explain.what: Every archive you built for the App Store or ad-hoc distribution, with its dSYM debug symbols (Details lists them).
explain.why: An old archive is the only way to symbolicate crash reports from that build, unless its dSYMs were uploaded (App Store Connect, Crashlytics).
explain.after: Gone. You can rebuild the same commit, but the new dSYM won't match crashes from the old build.
explain.keep: Archives of versions still in users' hands whose dSYMs aren't uploaded anywhere.

entries.label: Emulator system images
entries.note: Only used by emulators (AVDs). If you test on a physical device, these are dormant. ~2–3 GB per API level.

explain.what: Android OS images the emulator boots, one per API level and ABI, 2–3 GB each (Details lists them).
explain.why: Only emulators need them; a physical device doesn't.
explain.after: SDK Manager downloads an image again when you create an emulator that needs it.
explain.keep: An AVD you use runs on one of them.

entries.label: Emulator binary
entries.note: Useless without system images and an AVD.

explain.what: The emulator program itself (SDK Tools › Android Emulator).
explain.why: Without system images and an AVD it does nothing; with them it is what runs them.
explain.after: SDK Manager reinstalls it on request.
explain.keep: You run emulators.

entries.label: Android virtual devices (AVDs)
entries.note: Each emulator's disk, one per device — Details lists them and removes the device's .ini with it, so Device Manager stays clean. Recreate from Device Manager.

explain.what: Android virtual devices: each emulator's disk image and configuration, with the .ini Device Manager reads (Details lists them).
explain.why: An AVD is a test device; its state — installed apps, accounts, data — exists nowhere else.
explain.after: Device Manager creates a new one in a minute; it starts factory-fresh.
explain.keep: An emulator with test data you rely on.

entries.label: Android NDK
entries.note: Only projects with native (C/C++) code need it. The info lists installed versions and any project that references one.

explain.what: The Native Development Kit — C and C++ toolchains for Android — one folder per version, around 1 GB each.
explain.why: Only projects with native code, or a dependency that builds some, need it; Details lists the versions and the projects that name one.
explain.after: SDK Manager, or Gradle, downloads the version a project asks for.
explain.keep: A project's build files name an installed version.

entries.label: Android SDK sources
entries.note: Used only for jumping into framework source in the IDE.

explain.what: Source code of the Android framework, per API level, for browsing in the IDE.
explain.why: Only used to jump into framework source; nothing builds against it.
explain.after: Android Studio offers to download sources again when you open a framework file.

entries.label: SDK platforms + build-tools
entries.note: Every Android build needs these. Manage versions in SDK Manager.

explain.what: The SDK platforms, build-tools and platform-tools every Android build needs.
explain.why: Removing them breaks every Android build until SDK Manager reinstalls them; nothing is gained.
explain.keep: Always; retire old versions in SDK Manager.

entries.label: Gradle dependency cache
entries.note: Downloaded dependencies and build caches. The next build fetches what it needs.

explain.what: Downloaded dependencies (jars, AARs), transformed artifacts and build caches for every Gradle project.
explain.why: Gradle re-resolves anything missing from the repositories; nothing of yours is in here.
explain.after: The next build of each project downloads its dependencies again — minutes, more on a slow line.
explain.keep: You're about to build offline.

entries.label: Gradle distributions
entries.note: One Gradle per version any project ever requested.

explain.what: One Gradle distribution per version any project's wrapper ever asked for.
explain.why: The wrapper downloads whatever version a project pins.
explain.after: The next build of each project downloads its Gradle version again.

entries.label: Gradle-managed JDKs
entries.note: JDKs Gradle downloaded because projects asked for a Java version you didn't have.

explain.what: JDKs Gradle's toolchain support downloaded because projects asked for a Java version you didn't have installed.
explain.why: The projects that asked for them still need them, and Gradle downloads the same JDK again on the next build, so nothing is gained.
explain.keep: Always; install a JDK you manage yourself if you'd rather Gradle didn't.

entries.label: .NET NuGet cache
entries.note: Every package version ever restored. dotnet restore brings back what a project needs.

explain.what: Every NuGet package version any .NET project restored, one folder per package and version.
explain.why: dotnet restore downloads what a project needs; the folder is a cache.
explain.after: The next build of each project restores its packages again.

entries.label: npm cache
entries.note: Downloaded package tarballs. npm install fetches again as needed.

explain.what: npm's content-addressable cache of every package tarball it ever downloaded.
explain.why: npm only uses it to skip downloads; npm cache clean --force does the same.
explain.after: The next npm install in each project downloads again.

entries.label: Yarn cache
entries.note: Downloaded packages. yarn install fetches again as needed.

explain.what: Yarn's global cache of downloaded packages.
explain.why: A download cache; yarn cache clean does the same.
explain.after: The next yarn install in each project downloads again.

entries.label: Bun install cache
entries.note: Downloaded packages. bun install fetches again as needed.

explain.what: Bun's global cache of downloaded packages.
explain.why: A download cache; bun pm cache rm does the same.
explain.after: The next bun install in each project downloads again.

entries.label: Dart / Flutter pub cache
entries.note: Every package version ever fetched. flutter pub get brings back what a project needs.

explain.what: Every Dart and Flutter package version ever fetched, plus git checkouts of packages pulled from repositories.
explain.why: A download cache; flutter pub get restores what a project needs.
explain.after: The next pub get in each project downloads again.
explain.keep: Globally activated tools (dart pub global) live here too and would need reactivating.

entries.label: Maven repository
entries.note: Every artifact ever resolved. The next build downloads what it needs.

explain.what: Maven's local repository: every artifact any Maven or Gradle build ever resolved.
explain.why: A download cache; the next build fetches what it needs from the remote repositories.
explain.after: The next build of each project downloads its dependencies again.
explain.keep: You install your own artifacts locally (mvn install) and other projects depend on them.

entries.label: conda package cache
entries.note: Downloaded packages kept after install. conda clean --all does the same.

explain.what: Packages conda downloaded and unpacked, kept after installing into environments.
explain.why: Environments hard-link into this cache, but conda re-downloads anything an environment needs; conda clean --all does the same.
explain.after: Creating or updating an environment downloads packages again.

entries.label: pnpm store
entries.note: Downloaded packages; each project's node_modules is linked from it. pnpm install refills it.

explain.what: pnpm's content-addressable store; every project's node_modules is linked from it.
explain.why: A download cache by design: pnpm store prune removes unused packages, and pnpm install refills the rest.
explain.after: Run pnpm install in each project before its next build; it downloads and relinks what the project needs.

entries.label: CocoaPods cache
entries.note: Downloaded pod sources. pod install fetches again as needed.

explain.what: CocoaPods' download cache of pod sources.
explain.why: A download cache; pod install fetches what a Podfile needs.
explain.after: The next pod install in each project downloads again.

entries.label: Rust registry
entries.note: Downloaded crates and the registry index. cargo build fetches again as needed.

explain.what: Downloaded crate sources and the crates.io index.
explain.why: A download cache; cargo fetches what a project's lockfile names.
explain.after: The next cargo build in each project downloads again.

entries.label: Go module cache
entries.note: Downloaded modules. go build fetches again; go clean -modcache does the same.

explain.what: Downloaded Go modules, one read-only folder per module version, with the download cache.
explain.why: A download cache; go clean -modcache does the same.
explain.after: The next go build in each project downloads again.

entries.label: pip cache
entries.note: Downloaded wheels. pip install fetches again as needed.

explain.what: Wheels pip built or downloaded, and the HTTP responses it cached.
explain.why: A download cache; pip cache purge does the same.
explain.after: The next pip install downloads, and may rebuild, the wheels it needs.

entries.label: Node versions (nvm)
entries.note: Remove old ones with: nvm uninstall VERSION.

explain.what: Every Node version nvm installed, each with its own global packages.
explain.why: Installed toolchains, not a cache: a project's .nvmrc or a global tool may need an old version, and nvm should remove them so it forgets them too.
explain.after: nvm uninstall removes one version; nvm install brings it back, without its global packages.
explain.keep: The versions your projects' .nvmrc files name.

entries.label: Docker Desktop VM disk
entries.note: Grows to its high-water mark and never shrinks. Reclaim with: docker system prune -a, then Docker → Settings → Resources → Clean/Purge data.

explain.what: The disk image of Docker Desktop's Linux VM; every image, container and volume lives inside it.
explain.why: Deleting the file from outside Docker corrupts Docker's view of it; Docker's own prune and purge shrink it safely.
explain.after: docker system prune -a removes unused images and containers; Clean / Purge data resets Docker completely, and volumes with data are lost.
explain.keep: Volumes hold databases you haven't backed up.

entries.label: Rust toolchains (rustup)
entries.note: One folder per installed toolchain, 1–2 GB each — Details lists them. rustup reinstalls a toolchain on demand; the active one is named by `rustup show`.

explain.what: The Rust toolchains rustup installed, one folder per channel and version, 1–2 GB each (Details lists them).
explain.why: rustup reinstalls a toolchain on demand; only the active one, named by rustup show, is in use.
explain.after: The next build that needs a removed toolchain triggers its download again.
explain.keep: The active toolchain and any a project's rust-toolchain file pins.

entries.label: CocoaPods specs repos
entries.note: The podspec index clones. Since CocoaPods 1.8 the CDN replaces the multi-GB master clone; deleting a folder is what `pod repo remove` does.

explain.what: Clones of podspec repositories, one folder each; the master clone alone can be several GB.
explain.why: Since CocoaPods 1.8 the CDN serves specs, so the clones are only needed by Podfiles that name a git source; deleting one is what pod repo remove does.
explain.after: A Podfile that still names a git spec source clones it again on the next pod install.

entries.label: SDKMAN archives
entries.note: Downloaded JDK, Gradle and Kotlin archives kept after install. Re-downloaded if a version is reinstalled; installed SDKs are untouched.

explain.what: The JDK, Gradle, Kotlin and other archives SDKMAN downloaded, kept after installing.
explain.why: Installed SDKs live elsewhere; the archives only save a download on reinstall.
explain.after: Reinstalling a version downloads it again; nothing installed changes.

entries.label: Terraform plugin cache
entries.note: Provider binaries shared across projects. `terraform init` fetches them again.

explain.what: Provider binaries Terraform cached to share across projects.
explain.why: A download cache; terraform init fetches providers again.
explain.after: The next terraform init in each project downloads its providers.

entries.label: minikube image cache
entries.note: Kubernetes images and ISOs kept for new clusters. Re-downloaded on the next `minikube start`; running clusters live elsewhere.

explain.what: Kubernetes images and ISOs minikube keeps for creating new clusters.
explain.why: A download cache; running clusters live elsewhere and keep running.
explain.after: The next minikube start that needs a missing image downloads it.

entries.label: Next.js caches in project folders
entries.note: Build output and compiler cache. next dev or next build recreates it.

explain.what: .next folders — Next.js build output and its compiler cache inside each project.
explain.why: next dev or next build recreates them entirely from your source.
explain.after: The next start of each project builds again.

entries.label: Android build output in project folders
entries.note: android/app/build and android/build. Regenerated by the next Gradle build.

explain.what: The android/app/build and android/build folders of each project — Gradle's output.
explain.why: Regenerated by the next Gradle build from your source.
explain.after: The next build of each project is a full one.

entries.label: iOS build output in project folders
entries.note: Xcode output of React Native, Flutter and Capacitor projects. Regenerated by the next build.

explain.what: The build folder under each project's ios/ — Xcode output of React Native, Flutter and Capacitor projects.
explain.why: Regenerated by the next Xcode build from your source.
explain.after: The next build of each project is a full one.

entries.label: .NET bin/ and obj/ in project folders
entries.note: Only folders next to a .csproj are matched. Regenerated by dotnet build.

explain.what: bin/ and obj/ folders next to a .csproj — the compiler's output and intermediates.
explain.why: Regenerated by dotnet build; only folders beside a project file are matched, so a bin/ of your own is safe.
explain.after: The next build of each project is a full one.

entries.label: node_modules in project folders
entries.note: npm install brings each one back. Delete for projects you're not actively in.

explain.what: Each project's installed npm, pnpm or yarn dependencies.
explain.why: One install from the lockfile restores them; the code you wrote is elsewhere.
explain.after: Run npm install (or pnpm, yarn) in the project before working in it again — minutes per project.
explain.keep: Projects you are working in this week.

entries.label: CocoaPods Pods/ in project folders
entries.note: pod install brings them back.

explain.what: Each project's installed CocoaPods, restored from Podfile.lock.
explain.why: One pod install restores them; the code you wrote is elsewhere.
explain.after: Run pod install in the project before its next build.
explain.keep: Projects you are working in this week.

entries.label: Claude Code session transcripts
entries.note: Session transcripts (claude --resume) and the per-project memory notes Claude keeps.

explain.what: Claude Code's session transcripts, one file per session per project — and the auto-memory notes Claude keeps per project.
explain.why: Transcripts only serve claude --resume and the session picker; the memory notes are small but are what Claude remembers about each project.
explain.after: Old sessions can't be resumed and Claude forgets its per-project notes; new sessions record as before.
explain.keep: Sessions you may want to resume, or memory notes you've built up.

entries.label: Codex CLI sessions and logs
entries.note: Past sessions and logs — and Codex's config and login, which you'd set up again.

explain.what: Codex CLI's session logs and history — and its config and login.
explain.why: The sessions are only for looking back at old runs, but the whole folder goes, config and credentials included.
explain.after: Codex starts fresh: sign in and set your config again. Old sessions can't be resumed.
explain.keep: You'd rather not sign in again.

entries.label: Gemini CLI sessions and cache
entries.note: Past sessions and cache — and Gemini's settings and login, which you'd set up again.

explain.what: Gemini CLI's session history and cache — and its settings and login.
explain.why: The history is only for looking back, but the whole folder goes, settings and credentials included.
explain.after: Gemini CLI starts fresh: sign in and set it up again.
explain.keep: You'd rather not sign in again.

entries.label: Antigravity data
entries.note: Sessions, extensions and settings. Antigravity starts fresh; sign in again.

explain.what: Antigravity's local data: sessions, extensions, caches and settings.
explain.why: Nothing you wrote is in here, but the IDE starts from scratch afterwards.
explain.after: Antigravity starts fresh: sign in, reinstall extensions, redo settings.
explain.keep: You use Antigravity.

entries.label: Cursor data
entries.note: Extensions, settings and session data. Cursor starts fresh; extensions reinstall.

explain.what: Cursor's extensions, settings and session data.
explain.why: Nothing you wrote is in here, but the editor starts from scratch afterwards.
explain.after: Cursor starts fresh: extensions reinstall from settings sync or by hand.
explain.keep: You use Cursor.

entries.label: Notion local cache
entries.note: Re-syncs from the cloud. Quit Notion first.

explain.what: Notion's offline copy of your workspaces and its caches.
explain.why: Everything re-syncs from Notion's servers; only offline access and a fast first launch are lost until then.
explain.after: Notion downloads your workspaces again on the next launch. Quit it first.

entries.label: Steam data
entries.note: Installed games are the bulk. Uninstall single games from inside Steam instead.

explain.what: Steam's installed games, shader caches and the client itself.
explain.why: The games are the bulk; each downloads again from your library, but that is tens of GB per game.
explain.after: Steam reinstalls itself on the next launch; games download again when you install them.
explain.keep: Games you play — uninstall single games from inside Steam instead.

entries.label: Spotify cache
entries.note: Streamed audio kept for replay. Downloads for offline listening are elsewhere and untouched.

explain.what: Audio Spotify kept after streaming so replays don't download again.
explain.why: A cache; songs downloaded for offline listening are stored elsewhere and untouched.
explain.after: Songs stream from the network again as you play them.

entries.label: iPhone / iPad backups
entries.note: Local Finder backups, one per device — often the single biggest thing on a Mac. Details names each device. Needs Full Disk Access to measure.

explain.what: Finder (formerly iTunes) backups of iPhones and iPads, one folder per device, often 10–50 GB each (Details names them).
explain.why: A backup is the only copy if the device is lost — unless iCloud Backup is on for it.
explain.after: The next Finder backup of that device starts from scratch.
explain.keep: The device isn't backed up to iCloud, or you no longer have it and the backup holds its data.

entries.label: Ollama models
entries.itemsCmd: ollama list 2>/dev/null | awk 'NR>1 { s=$3; u=$4; kb=(u=="GB")?s*1048576:(u=="MB")?s*1024:s/1024; printf "%s\t%s\t%d\n", $1, $1, kb }'
entries.note: Several GB per model. Details lists them; ollama pull brings one back.

linux.itemsCmd: ollama list 2>/dev/null | awk 'NR>1 { s=$3; u=$4; kb=(u=="GB")?s*1048576:(u=="MB")?s*1024:s/1024; printf "%s\t%s\t%d\n", $1, $1, kb }'

explain.what: Model weights Ollama downloaded, several GB each (Details lists them).
explain.why: ollama pull brings any of them back, but each is a large download.
explain.after: ollama pull downloads a model again when you ask for it.
explain.keep: Models you use.

entries.label: Mail attachment downloads
entries.note: Attachments you opened from Mail; the originals stay in the messages. Needs Full Disk Access to measure.

explain.what: Attachments you opened or Quick Looked from Mail; the originals stay in the messages.
explain.why: A cache of copies; Mail writes a new copy the next time you open an attachment.
explain.after: Opening an attachment writes a fresh copy.

entries.label: Microsoft Teams cache
entries.note: Rebuilt on the next launch; quit Teams first. Needs Full Disk Access to measure.

explain.what: Microsoft Teams' cache of images, files and web content.
explain.why: Rebuilt on the next launch; chats and files live on the server.
explain.after: Teams starts a little slower once, then refills the cache. Quit it first.

entries.label: Messages attachments
entries.note: Photos and files from every conversation. Trim from inside Messages (a conversation → Info → Photos) so iCloud stays in sync; Backspacer only measures this. Needs Full Disk Access.

explain.what: Photos, videos and files from every Messages conversation.
explain.why: Real data that iCloud keeps in sync; deleting the folder by hand desyncs Messages, so Backspacer only measures it.
explain.after: Trim from inside Messages — a conversation › Info › Photos — and the change syncs to your other devices.
explain.keep: Attachments you want in Messages.

entries.label: Safari data
entries.note: Clear from inside Safari: History → Clear History. Needs Full Disk Access to measure.

explain.what: Safari's container: history, website data and caches, and offline Reading List items.
explain.why: Real data and cache mixed; Safari's own Clear History and website-data tools remove the safe parts.
explain.after: Safari › History › Clear History clears history and caches; Settings › Privacy › Manage Website Data removes per-site data.
explain.keep: History and logins you rely on.

entries.label: Telegram media cache
entries.note: Clear from inside Telegram: Settings → Data and Storage → Storage Usage.

explain.what: Media Telegram downloaded for chats: photos, videos, files.
explain.why: Telegram re-downloads media from its servers, but only its own tool clears the cache without confusing it.
explain.after: Telegram › Settings › Data and Storage › Storage Usage clears the cache; media downloads again on view.

entries.label: Parallels virtual machines
entries.note: Whole VMs, tens of GB each. Delete from Parallels Control Center so it forgets them too.

explain.what: Parallels virtual machines, tens of GB each.
explain.why: Whole machines with their own disks; Parallels Control Center should delete one so it forgets it too.
explain.after: Remove from Parallels Control Center; a deleted VM is gone with everything installed inside it.
explain.keep: Any VM you still boot.

entries.label: UTM virtual machines
entries.note: Delete from inside UTM. Needs Full Disk Access to measure.

explain.what: UTM virtual machines, each with its disk image.
explain.why: Whole machines; delete from inside UTM so its library stays in sync.
explain.after: A deleted VM is gone with everything installed inside it.
explain.keep: Any VM you still boot.

entries.label: Vagrant boxes
entries.note: Base boxes, GBs each — Details lists them. `vagrant up` downloads a box again; VMs already created from one keep running.

explain.what: Base boxes Vagrant downloaded, gigabytes each (Details lists them).
explain.why: Boxes are templates: VMs already created from one keep running, and vagrant up downloads a box again.
explain.after: The next vagrant up of a project without its box downloads it again.

entries.label: Screenshots and screen recordings
entries.sizeCmd: { find ~/Screenshots -type f -print0 2>/dev/null; find ~/Desktop -maxdepth 1 \( -name '*.mov' -o -name '*.png' -o -name '*.jpg' \) -print0 2>/dev/null; } | xargs -0 du -sk 2>/dev/null | awk '{s+=$1} END {print s+0}'
entries.note: Recordings are the bulk. Review in Finder.

explain.what: Screenshots and screen recordings saved to the Desktop, or the folder you chose in Screenshot › Options.
explain.why: Your files; recordings run to hundreds of MB each. Backspacer never deletes your files.
explain.after: Review them in Finder and trash what you don't need.
explain.keep: Anything you haven't looked at yet.

entries.label: Downloads
entries.note: Your files. Installers (.dmg, .pkg) are usually the safe part to trash.

explain.what: Everything you downloaded: installers, archives, PDFs, exports.
explain.why: Your files, of mixed value only you can judge. Backspacer never deletes your files.
explain.after: Review in Finder; installers (.dmg, .pkg) and archives you've already unpacked are usually the safe part.
explain.keep: Anything you haven't sorted yet.

entries.label: Time Machine local snapshots
entries.note: macOS purges these itself under storage pressure, and the free-space figure already counts them, so thinning gains nothing visible. Size isn't reported; Details shows how many exist. If a tool needs real (not purgeable) space: sudo tmutil thinlocalsnapshots / 999999999999 4

explain.what: APFS snapshots Time Machine keeps on the internal disk between backups.
explain.why: macOS deletes them itself under storage pressure and already counts them as purgeable, so thinning them changes nothing you can see.
explain.keep: Always, unless a tool insists on real free space — then sudo tmutil thinlocalsnapshots / 999999999999 4.

entries.label: Apple Intelligence & Siri models
entries.note: Stay on disk even with Apple Intelligence off. SIP-protected; macOS purges them itself under storage pressure.

explain.what: On-device Apple Intelligence and Siri models under /System/Library/AssetsV2.
explain.why: SIP-protected system assets that stay even with Apple Intelligence off; macOS purges them itself under storage pressure.
explain.keep: Always; there is no supported way to remove them.

entries.label: Apple developer documentation
entries.note: Offline developer documentation, downloaded and purged by macOS itself.

explain.what: Apple developer documentation downloaded for offline use, as a system asset.
explain.why: SIP-protected; macOS downloads and purges it itself.
explain.keep: Always; there is no supported way to remove it by hand.

entries.label: Linguistic data
entries.note: Language data for spelling, prediction and dictation. macOS manages it.

explain.what: Language data for spelling, predictive text and dictation, one set per language you've enabled.
explain.why: SIP-protected; macOS adds and removes it with your keyboard and language settings.
explain.keep: Always; remove languages in System Settings › Keyboard instead.

entries.label: apt package cache
entries.note: The .deb files apt downloaded for every install. apt keeps them after installing; apt-get clean removes the same thing.

explain.what: The .deb packages apt downloaded for every install and upgrade, kept afterwards.
explain.why: Installed packages don't need their .deb; apt-get clean removes the same files.
explain.after: A reinstall or a downgrade downloads the package again.

entries.label: dnf package cache
entries.note: Downloaded packages and repository metadata on Fedora and friends. Rebuilt on the next dnf run.

explain.what: Packages dnf downloaded and the repository metadata it fetched.
explain.why: Installed packages don't need them; dnf clean all removes the same.
explain.after: The next dnf run fetches metadata again; a reinstall downloads the package again.

entries.label: snap download cache
entries.note: Snap packages kept after installation. snapd re-downloads what an update needs.

explain.what: Snap packages kept after installation, including old revisions.
explain.why: snapd re-downloads whatever an update needs; installed snaps are elsewhere.
explain.after: The next snap refresh downloads what it needs.

entries.label: Thumbnail cache
entries.note: Every file manager's preview images. Regenerated as folders are opened.

explain.what: Preview images every file manager generated for files it showed.
explain.why: Regenerated as folders are opened; a cache by definition.
explain.after: Folders show generic icons until their thumbnails are regenerated.

entries.label: Trash
entries.note: Your Trash. Emptying it here is the same as emptying it in the file manager.

explain.what: What you moved to the Trash and haven't emptied.
explain.why: You already discarded it; Backspacer only empties the bin.
explain.after: Gone for good, exactly as emptying the Trash in the file manager.

entries.label: systemd journal
entries.note: System and service logs, often gigabytes on a long-lived install. journald starts a fresh journal after removal; keep it if you are debugging something.

explain.what: systemd's binary logs for the system and every service, often gigabytes on a long-lived install.
explain.why: Logs matter only while you're debugging something; journald starts a fresh journal afterwards.
explain.after: The journal starts empty. journalctl --vacuum-size trims it more gently.
explain.keep: You are debugging a problem and need the history.

entries.label: Temporary files
entries.note: Every app's scratch files. Files still in use are skipped; the rest is recreated on demand.

explain.what: Every app's scratch files in the user's temp folder.
explain.why: Temporary by definition; files still in use are skipped, the rest is recreated on demand.
explain.after: Apps recreate what they need.

entries.label: Windows Update downloads
entries.note: Update packages already installed or waiting. Windows re-downloads whatever it still needs.

explain.what: Update packages Windows Update downloaded — already installed or waiting to install.
explain.why: Windows re-downloads whatever it still needs; installed updates don't need the package.
explain.after: Pending updates download again on the next check.

entries.label: Delivery Optimization cache
entries.note: Update and Store downloads kept to share with other PCs. Refilled by the next update.

explain.what: Update and Store downloads Windows keeps to share with other PCs on the network.
explain.why: A cache refilled by the next update; sharing only saves other machines a download.
explain.after: The next update refills it.

entries.label: Crash dumps
entries.note: Memory dumps written when an app crashes. Useful only while reporting that crash.

explain.what: Memory dumps Windows wrote when apps crashed.
explain.why: Useful only while reporting that crash to the app's developer.
explain.after: Gone; the next crash writes a new dump.
explain.keep: You are about to report a crash.
